html:
The Lemhi Shoshone, or Agaidika, "salmon eaters", are a band of the Northern Shoshone who lived in the Lemhi and Salmon river valleys of eastern Idaho. They spoke Shoshoni, a Uto-Aztecan language.

They fished the salmon runs, gathered roots and, after getting horses in the 1700s (horses on the Plains), crossed the mountains to hunt bison. Sacagawea, who guided the Lewis and Clark Expedition, was born among them. In August 1805 the expedition reached the Lemhi Shoshone, and Sacagawea found that their chief Cameahwait was her brother; his horses let the party cross the Rockies.

A reservation in the Lemhi Valley was set up in 1875, but in 1907 the government closed it and moved the people to Fort Hall, where they joined the Shoshone-Bannock tribes.
